title: Report on Studying Abroad at Duke University
paragraphs: Sitting at my desk now writing this report, those intense days come back to me: the struggle with the TOEFL before my study abroad was decided, the pre-departure training sessions with the other members after it was decided, and the many memories of the United States.

What I struggled with most was English. I had thought I had prepared reasonably well for English in Japan through TOEFL study and the like, but what I actually heard on site, such as each person's different pronunciation and so-called slang, was more difficult than I had imagined and I was very confused. However, perhaps because I could not move forward unless I understood English, I gradually came to understand it as time went by.

In my three-month clerkship at Duke University, I rotated for about one month each through cardiology, neurosurgery and neuroradiology. The first, cardiology, was frankly a very hard clerkship. I left home at 5:30 in the morning and took the bus to the university, and came home using the university's late-night taxi. The students' role was mainly to take consults from other departments, and in addition there were lectures on how to do the physical examination twice a week. It was a clerkship in which one kept working all day, and it was physically tough, but in fact I looked forward to going to the university every day. I think this was above all because studying while discussing this and that about our assigned patients together with the local students was so fulfilling. Spending time with them, who were studying with high motivation, was very stimulating.

My second clerkship was neurosurgery. I had heard that the neurosurgery department at Duke University is highly rated even within the United States, so I was greatly looking forward to it, and it was beyond my expectations. There were more than ten operations every day, and I could choose the operations I was interested in and take part, learning the use of various instruments and techniques such as suturing. However, in this neurosurgery clerkship I was able to gain an even bigger experience than that. It was that I was allowed to take part in a workshop held in Florida. Neurosurgeons from all over the world gathered at this workshop, stayed at a hotel for three days, and improved their skills while being instructed by professors from Duke University in front of cadavers. I was surprised that not only residents but also doctors who had already built careers as neurosurgeons for many years, such as heads of departments at large hospitals and university professors, took part. I strongly felt that the sight of these doctors constantly polishing themselves is something I must never forget when I become a doctor in the future. The dinners held every night were also a great deal of fun, as they were occasions to hear about the doctors' various experiences.

My last clerkship department was neuroradiology. The clerkship in radiology was a form in which I sat right next to the doctor reading the images, tried reading them myself, and asked questions on the spot. It was of course good study for image reading, but for me it was also a meaningful place to learn English. In addition, the doctors taught me carefully, one by one, whatever questions I asked, until I understood. It seemed that they felt not only a sense of responsibility for training doctors but also that they themselves enjoyed teaching.

Interaction with the Duke University students outside the clerkships is also one of my unforgettable experiences. With them I spent time almost every day in the free time between clerkships and at mealtimes, and we talked about all sorts of things, from serious talk about the differences between medicine and medical education in Japan and the United States and what kind of doctor we want to become, to trivial so-called small talk and silly jokes. The time spent eating Krispy Kreme doughnuts, which originated in North Carolina, where Duke University is located (I heard that there was a line at the opening day in Nagoya), together with Starbucks coffee in the hospital cafeteria made me feel that I was in a foreign country. It was truly sad to part from them. However, I think the existence of those who, as doctors, will be in their respective places around the world will always encourage me, giving me pride and courage in being one of their companions.

I am very grateful to have been given such a valuable experience as a medical student. I am sure that this experience will have a great influence on how I live from now on. I would like to take this opportunity to sincerely thank the professors at Nagoya University, the staff of the Academic Affairs Division and the International Exchange Office, the doctors and students at Duke University, the staff of the international office, Fred and Jenny, who kindly hosted me in their home, my fellow exchange students who studied hard together with me, and my parents, who supported me both financially and emotionally, for supporting me so that my study abroad could be carried out safely.
